title: The AI Lawyer
answer: Ten areas where artificial intelligence is changing legal work: discovery, contracts, research, corporate governance, intellectual property, litigation strategy, firm operations, privacy, the law being written now, and the security audits underneath all of it.

children.name: E-Discovery and Large-Scale Document Analysis
children.blurb: Predictive coding, cross-lingual review, audio and video evidence, privilege logging, and sentiment analysis of corporate messaging.

children.name: Contract Lifecycle and Algorithmic Drafting
children.blurb: Clause extraction, agent redlining, executable contracts, obligation tracking and template generation.

children.name: Legal Research and Case Strategy
children.blurb: Retrieval-grounded research, adversarial statutory reading, brief drafting, citation auditing and jurisdictional anomalies.

children.name: Corporate Governance and Regulatory Compliance
children.blurb: Board advisory, supply chain and ESG auditing, insider trading detection, regulatory change mapping and merger modelling.

children.name: Intellectual Property and Trademark Strategy
children.blurb: Clearance searching, trademark filing, licensing synthetic assets, patent claim drafting and infringement detection.

children.name: Litigation Prediction and Judicial Analytics
children.blurb: Judicial and opposing counsel analytics, settlement valuation, jury selection and live testimony cross-referencing.

children.name: Legal Operations, Infrastructure and Security
children.blurb: Local model deployment, secure networking, billing, knowledge management and client intake.

children.name: Data Privacy and Cyber-Regulatory Compliance
children.blurb: Privacy framework harmonisation, breach response, cross-border transfers, AI supply chain risk and biometric law.

children.name: Emerging Legal Frameworks
children.blurb: Machine authorship, autonomous entities, multi-agent liability, deepfake evidence and the right to an explanation.

children.name: AI Security Audits and Enterprise Enablement
children.blurb: Enablement audits, threat modelling for legal models, data loss prevention, shadow AI and bias testing.

sections.body: This field covers ten areas where artificial intelligence is doing legal work today, not in theory. In discovery, software reads millions of documents to find relevant material faster than human review teams. In contracts, systems draft clauses, flag risky terms, and track obligations across a company's agreements. Legal research tools now answer natural language questions with cited case law, and some firms use analytics to estimate how a judge might rule. Corporate teams use AI to monitor regulatory changes, while intellectual property groups search trademarks and prior art at scale. The site tracks 732 AI tools across these functions, which gives a sense of how much is already in use.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. E-discovery is the most mature area, with courts generally accepting machine review as reasonable. Contract drafting and legal research are widely used but still require lawyer oversight because models can miss nuance or cite cases that do not exist. Litigation prediction remains limited, since past rulings do not capture the full facts of a new case. The site records 142 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, and 29 AI case law precedents, which shows the law itself is still being settled. Privacy and security audits are growing but not standardized, and honest limits include bias in training data, hallucinated citations, and the difficulty of explaining a model's reasoning to a judge or client.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages move from the most established uses to the least settled. A reader looking for how machines handle evidence would start with E-Discovery and Large-Scale Document Analysis, then see how the same techniques feed Contract Lifecycle and Algorithmic Drafting. Legal Research and Case Strategy and Litigation Prediction and Judicial Analytics cover the analytical side, while Corporate Governance and Regulatory Compliance and Data Privacy and Cyber-Regulatory Compliance address the rules companies must follow. Intellectual Property and Trademark Strategy sits at the center of the current disputes, given the 92 IP lawsuits tracked. Legal Operations, Infrastructure and Security and AI Security Audits and Enterprise Enablement explain how firms and legal departments run these tools safely. Emerging Legal Frameworks is where a reader would go to understand the 6,823 state bills and the law being written now.
